Evidence

The Science

The voice on this site is personal. The claims are checked. Here is what the research says, in plain language, with every source so you can read it yourself.

Ten findings worth knowing

  1. Most people recover. About one US adult in eleven reports having resolved a significant alcohol or drug problem. More
  2. Meetings work. The most rigorous review to date found AA and twelve-step programmes produce more continuous abstinence than other established treatments. More
  3. The active ingredient is people. Much of the benefit comes from building a sober social circle, and alternatives to twelve-step groups work about as well for those who get involved. More
  4. Age mix matters early on. Young adults did better at first in meetings with more people their own age. More
  5. Cravings pass. Mindfulness-based relapse prevention, built around urge surfing, outperformed standard approaches at twelve months. More
  6. The brain heals. Imaging studies show structural recovery during abstinence, starting within weeks and continuing past a year. More
  7. Relapse is common and not final. Rates are similar to other long-term conditions, and most people who recover needed more than one attempt. More
  8. Helping helps the helper. People who helped others in recovery were about twice as likely to stay sober the following year. More
  9. Thrill-seeking is a trait you can aim. It peaks in the late teens, predicts substance use, and responds to programmes that give it somewhere to go. More
  10. Sport is not automatically protective. Young people in sport use fewer drugs but often drink more. Club culture decides which way it goes. More

How this site handles evidence

  • Systematic reviews and large trials are preferred. A single study is described as a single study.
  • Observational findings are labelled as such. A link between two things doesn't prove one causes the other.
  • Where evidence is mixed or missing, the page says so. First Summer, for example, is built on research but has not itself been tested.
  • Personal experience is presented as personal experience.
  • Research moves. If something here is out of date or wrong, I want to fix it.

None of this is medical advice. A study describes what happened on average to the people in it. A doctor who knows you can tell you what applies to you.
